title: Yes means yes
hook: truthfulness in all speech, not just under oath

segments.voice: Yesterday, the little ones: a child set in the middle of the disciples, and a warning about millstones. Your line was protect the little ones.

"I swear, I'll be there at six." "Honestly, I loved it." "No, seriously, I'll pay you back." Listen to how much extra packaging people wrap around ordinary sentences to make them believable. As if a plain sentence, left on its own, might not be true. Jesus noticed the same habit in his own day, when people swore by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by their own heads, and quietly treated some oaths as more binding than others. His answer was short.

It's in the Sermon on the Mount. After telling his listeners not to swear at all, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Notice what that does. If you need an oath to be believed, it suggests your ordinary words are a lower grade of truth. Swearing creates two kinds of speech: the sworn kind you must keep, and the everyday kind you can bend. Jesus folds them back into one. Every word is meant to be the sworn kind. James, writing to early Christians, repeats it almost word for word: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." Christians have applied this in different ways. Quakers, Mennonites and some other churches take it literally and decline to swear oaths, even in court; they make a solemn affirmation instead. Other churches read Jesus as forbidding careless and manipulative oaths, not every oath. They point out that Paul calls God as his witness in his letters, and they allow oaths in court and at ordination. Both sides agree on the heart of it: a person whose plain word can be trusted without extra packaging. Yesterday's warning was about not making the little ones stumble. This one is about not making anyone guess. A yes that means yes. A no that means no. And no secret third option hidden behind the words.

Think of one thing you've said you would do that's still hanging, a call you promised, a favor, something you told a kid, and hold it plainly: no excuses, no reasons, just the yes you gave. Then notice how often your sentences reach for honestly or I swear, and whether they could stand on their own. If you pray, you can offer your words to God.
Yes means yes. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 5: let your yea be yea and your nay, nay, so that every plain word is as true as an oath.
Your line: plain truth. A plain yes, on its own, can be enough. See you soon.

fork.setup: you're a Quaker called as a witness. the clerk holds out a Bible and asks you to swear. what do you do?
options: make a solemn affirmation instead, and tell the truth.
fork.reveal: Quakers take "swear not at all" literally and affirm instead, where the court allows it. the point isn't to avoid the truth; it's that every word should already be true.

chat.says: If I don't say I swear, does that mean I don't really have to do it?
options: No. Jesus said let your yea be yea; every plain word should be as true as an oath.
Right. Only sworn promises count; ordinary words can bend a little if needed.
Kind of. A promise only binds you if you made it in a church or a court.
chat.meaning: Jesus folds sworn speech and everyday speech into one: let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay. A plain word should be trustworthy on its own.

affirmation.meaning: a solemn promise made instead of an oath

ordination.meaning: the service that makes someone a minister or priest
